title: Dedicated throughput SLA quantile + error-burn playbook
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Purpose: Define a clear, measurable, and legally-safe way to promise Dedicated throughput to customers, compute an intuitive error budget, and specify contractual credit language. This ticket captures the proposed measurement primitives, the burn-rate model for credits, autoscaler interlocks, and fleet controls that preserve isolation while enabling graceful degradation.

Scope: 1) Metric definition for 'Committed Throughput' (CTX) and the measurement window; 2) Error budget and credit computation algorithm; 3) Contract clause examples (customer-facing) and internal SRE remediation playbook; 4) Requirements for autoscaler behaviour and fleet controls to avoid SLA punching; 5) Ops/observability signals to report and validate SLA compliance.

Background: Customers on Dedicated contracts want predictable throughput for latency-sensitive features (chat, streaming) and large-batch workloads. Existing documents focus on throughput bands and credit buckets but do not standardize: quantile-based measurement, burst fair-use accounting, or the dynamic burn-rate used for partial breaches. This playbook balances legal simplicity, measurable obligations, and operational feasibility.
acceptance_criteria: Clear definition of Committed Throughput (CT): tokens-per-minute (TPM) and requests-per-minute (RPM) variants documented
Error budget math documented with examples and test vectors for monthly billing windows
Contract language with plain-English summary + legal appendix ready for review
Autoscaler/ops interlock spec that engineers can implement and SREs can validate
Dashboards and alerts wireframe linked and validated with an emulation test
decision_log: 2025-02-20: Chose tokens-per-minute (TPM) as primary throughput unit; RPM as secondary for conversational workloads where tokens vary widely.
2025-02-26: Adopted 1-minute sampling windows aggregated into a rolling 30-day window for commercial SLAs and a 7-day window for internal SRE early-warning detection.

2025-03-01: Selected quantile-based SLO anchor: CT is considered met if the 90th-percentile of 1-minute TPM samples across the measurement window >= committed TPM. Trade-off: 90th percentile is more forgiving than p50 but tighter than p95 for sustained guarantees; legal prefers simpler phrasing.

2025-03-04: Credit model chosen: proportional crediting based on weighted shortfall (see 'credit_formula' in this ticket). Legal accepts proportional credits rather than binary refunds to reduce dispute volume.
credit_formula: MonthlyCredit = MonthlyCharge * max(0, (CommittedTPM - ObservedEffectiveTPM) / CommittedTPM) * BurnFactor; where ObservedEffectiveTPM = 90thPercentile(1-minute TPM samples over billing window). BurnFactor tiers: 0.5 for <10% shortfall, 1.0 for 10-30% shortfall, 1.5 for >30% shortfall. Minimum credit threshold: credits only apply if ObservedEffectiveTPM < 0.95 * CommittedTPM over the 30-day window.
contract_excerpt:
Plain-language statement for customer-facing contract: 'Redwood Inference will provide a dedicated throughput commitment measured in tokens-per-minute (TPM). We measure throughput in 1-minute intervals and compute the 90th percentile over the applicable billing window. If the delivered throughput falls below your committed TPM, Redwood will apply proportionate service credits according to the published credit schedule. Credits are the sole and exclusive remedy for throughput shortfalls except as required by law.'

Appendix (technical): 'Committed Throughput (CT) is defined as the customer's committed TPM. ObservedEffectiveTPM is the 90th percentile of 1-minute TPM samples over the billing window. Credits are computed per the credit formula. Customer must submit claim within 45 days of the billing period. During widespread infrastructure events, Redwood will exclude minutes where a force majeure or cross-customer datacenter outage is in effect, subject to audit.'
autoscale_interlock: Requirements for autoscaler and reserved pool: 1) Preserve a reserved pool that cannot be preempted by non-reserved tenants when a customer has a CTX contract in the AZ/region; 2) Autoscaler must notify contract manager when transient provisioning cannot restore CT within 5 minutes so that escalation can start; 3) Capacity reclaim policies: if autoscaler scales down due to reclaim, it must respect min-serve floor equal to 70% of CT for at least 15 minutes unless a force-majeure condition applies; 4) Fallback routing: during partial fleet degradation, route traffic to alternate fleet variants while respecting data-residency constraints; such fallbacks do not constitute a breach if they keep ObservedEffectiveTPM above 95% of CT.
observability_requirements: 1) 1-minute TPM sampling for each customer on Dedicated; 2) rolling 7-day and 30-day aggregations including p50/p90/p99 of 1-minute windows; 3) automated claim detection: flag customers where p90 < 0.98*CT for 24 hours; 4) per-customer audit logs, incident timeline, and automated credit calculation output for legal review.
open_questions: Do we standardize on p90 vs p95 as the legal metric? (p90 selected as default in this ticket but requires Exec sign-off)

How to account for scheduled maintenance that impacts a small subset of minutes? Proposed: offer an opt-in scheduled-maintenance exclusion with advance notice and no credits if customer accepts window.
Should credits be capped for repeated breaches within a 90-day rolling period? Legal suggests a cap to avoid unlimited liability.
How to handle multi-region committed fleets where capacity is aggregated across regions vs strict per-region guarantees?
